They organised trade unions (AITUC, 1920, with its first president Lala Lajpat Rai) and peasant organisations (All India Kisan Sabha, 1936). They opposed the Quit India Movement in 1942 because of the 'People's War' line after the Soviet Union joined the Allies.

The Congress Socialist Party (CSP) was founded in 1934 within Congress by Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia, Minoo Masani and Achyut Patwardhan, to give the national movement a socialist direction. Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose were sympathetic to socialism. The left pushed Congress to adopt pro-peasant and pro-worker programmes (the Karachi resolution of 1931 on Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy, and the Faizpur agrarian programme of 1936).
Bhagat Singh became a leading revolutionary figure who linked anti-colonial struggle with radical political ideas.

Bhagat Singh (1907-1931), from Punjab, was influenced by the Ghadar movement, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) and socialist ideas. With Chandrashekhar Azad, Sukhdev and others, he reorganised the Hindustan Republican Association as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA, 1928), aiming for a socialist republic. To avenge Lala Lajpat Rai's death after a police lathi-charge during the Simon Commission protest, he and Rajguru killed police officer J. P. Saunders (1928).

On 8 April 1929, Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw harmless bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly, shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad', and allowed themselves to be arrested, to use the trial for propaganda ('to make the deaf hear'). In jail he went on hunger strike and wrote 'Why I am an Atheist'. He, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on 23 March 1931 in Lahore. He became a symbol of revolutionary courage and socialist ideals.
Surya Sen led revolutionary activity associated especially with the Chittagong Armoury Raid.

Surya Sen ('Masterda'), a schoolteacher, led the Indian Republican Army in Chittagong (now in Bangladesh). On 18 April 1930, his group raided the police and auxiliary force armouries in Chittagong, cut telegraph and railway lines and proclaimed a provisional revolutionary government. Many young men and women took part, including Ganesh Ghosh, Ananta Singh, Lokenath Bal and Kalpana Dutta.

After a battle at Jalalabad hills, where several revolutionaries were killed, the group continued guerrilla attacks. Pritilata Waddedar led an attack on the Pahartali European Club (1932) and took poison to avoid capture. Surya Sen was arrested in 1933 and hanged in January 1934. The raid showed the participation of women in revolutionary activity and inspired later generations.
The INA sought to fight British rule militarily and became associated particularly with Subhas Chandra Bose.

The INA (Azad Hind Fauj) was first formed in 1942 by Captain Mohan Singh, with Indian prisoners of war captured by Japan in Malaya and Singapore, with support from Rash Behari Bose's Indian Independence League. Subhas Chandra Bose, who had escaped from house arrest in 1941 and gone to Germany, arrived in Singapore in 1943 and took command. He formed the Provisional Government of Free India (Azad Hind) on 21 October 1943, gave the slogans 'Delhi Chalo' and 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom', and created the Rani of Jhansi Regiment under Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan (Sehgal).

The INA fought alongside the Japanese in the Imphal and Kohima campaigns (1944) in Manipur and Nagaland, but was defeated; Bose reportedly died in an air crash in Taiwan in August 1945. The British trial of INA officers (Shah Nawaz Khan, P. K. Sahgal and G. S. Dhillon) at the Red Fort (1945-1946) caused nationwide protests and showed that the loyalty of the Indian armed forces could no longer be relied upon, which hastened independence.
The Royal Indian Navy Mutiny of 1946 reflected serious unrest among naval ratings and occurred during the final phase of British rule.

On 18 February 1946, ratings (sailors) of the Royal Indian Navy on HMIS Talwar in Bombay went on strike against racial discrimination, poor food, low pay and the INA trials. The mutiny spread to about 78 ships and 20 shore establishments in Bombay, Karachi, Calcutta, Madras and elsewhere, involving about 20,000 ratings. The mutineers raised Congress, Muslim League and Communist flags together, and workers in Bombay struck in support.

The British used force; Congress leaders (Vallabhbhai Patel) and Jinnah persuaded the ratings to surrender on 23 February, as they feared indiscipline and violence. The mutiny showed the decline of British control over the armed forces and contributed to Britain's decision to send the Cabinet Mission and leave India.
Mahatma Gandhi transformed nationalism by bringing large numbers of ordinary people into organised non-violent mass movements.

Gandhi (1869-1948) developed satyagraha (truth-force, non-violent resistance) in South Africa (1893-1914) against racial discrimination. In India, he led local struggles in Champaran (1917, indigo farmers), Ahmedabad (1918, mill workers' strike) and Kheda (1918, peasants' revenue remission). He opposed the Rowlatt Act (1919) with a nationwide hartal; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) followed.

His methods - non-violence, non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting, constructive work (khadi, Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability, village industries) - and his simple lifestyle and use of religious symbols and Indian languages brought peasants, women, workers and ordinary people into the movement, transforming the Congress into a mass organisation. Historians debate his relationship with peasant radicalism and his compromises, but his role in creating a mass, non-violent national movement is undisputed.
Launched in 1920, Non-Cooperation encouraged withdrawal from colonial institutions and promoted non-violent resistance.

Causes: the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the inadequate Montagu-Chelmsford reforms (1919), the Hunter Committee's whitewash, and the Khilafat issue (Muslim anger at the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War). Gandhi joined the Khilafat leaders (the Ali brothers) and the Congress adopted the programme at Calcutta (September 1920) and Nagpur (December 1920).

Programme: surrender of titles, boycott of legislatures, law courts, government schools and colleges, and foreign cloth; promotion of swadeshi, khadi, national schools (Jamia Millia Islamia, Kashi Vidyapith), and panchayats; and possibly non-payment of taxes. There were strikes, peasant movements (Awadh, Malabar - the Mappila rebellion) and tribal movements. Gandhi promised 'swaraj within a year'. After a mob burned a police station at Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur) on 5 February 1922, killing 22 policemen, Gandhi called off the movement. It made Congress a mass party and spread nationalism to villages.
The movement openly challenged colonial laws, with the Salt March becoming its most famous symbol.

Background: the Simon Commission boycott (1928), the Nehru Report, and the Lahore Congress (December 1929) under Jawaharlal Nehru, which declared Purna Swaraj (complete independence) as the goal; 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day. Gandhi's eleven demands to the Viceroy were rejected. On 12 March 1930, he began the Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 followers, walking 240 miles to Dandi, where he broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

The movement spread: salt was made illegally, foreign cloth and liquor were boycotted, forest laws were broken, and taxes were refused. Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgars (Red Shirts) in the North-West Frontier, Rani Gaidinliu in Nagaland and Manipur, and C. Rajagopalachari's salt march in Tamil Nadu (Vedaranyam) were notable; over 90,000 were arrested. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) suspended it; Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference, which failed. The movement was resumed (1932) and withdrawn in 1934. It involved more women and a wider social base than Non-Cooperation.
The Quit India Movement of 1942 demanded an end to British rule and led to widespread resistance after Congress leaders were arrested.

After the failure of the Cripps Mission, the threat of Japanese invasion and growing discontent, the Congress passed the Quit India resolution at Bombay on 8 August 1942. Gandhi gave the call 'Do or Die'. The next morning, Gandhi and all major leaders were arrested.

The leaderless movement saw spontaneous protests, strikes, attacks on railway lines, police stations and government buildings, and the formation of parallel governments in Ballia (Uttar Pradesh), Tamluk (Bengal, Jatiya Sarkar) and Satara (Maharashtra, Prati Sarkar). Underground leaders included Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali and Usha Mehta (Congress Radio). The government crushed it with great force - over 100,000 arrests and about 1,000 deaths officially. The Muslim League and Communists did not support it. The movement showed the depth of nationalist feeling and made clear that British rule could not continue for long after the war.
Opposition to the all-British Simon Commission stimulated constitutional debate, while the Nehru Report proposed an Indian constitutional framework.

The Simon Commission (1927), appointed under the Government of India Act 1919 to review constitutional progress, had seven British members and no Indians. It was boycotted with black flags and the slogan 'Simon Go Back' when it arrived in 1928; Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in a lathi-charge in Lahore and died. Secretary of State Lord Birkenhead challenged Indians to produce an agreed constitution.

An All Parties Conference appointed a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru, which produced the Nehru Report (August 1928). It proposed dominion status, a federal structure, responsible government, a list of fundamental rights, universal adult franchise, joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities and linguistic provinces. Jinnah's 'Fourteen Points' (1929) rejected it, and young radicals (Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Bose) wanted complete independence. The Lahore Congress (1929) then adopted Purna Swaraj.
The Cripps Mission of 1942 offered constitutional proposals but failed to secure agreement with Indian political leaders.

In March 1942, with Japan advancing in Southeast Asia and under pressure from the USA and China, the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps to India. His proposals: dominion status after the war; a constituent assembly elected by provincial legislatures and nominated by princes; the right of any province to stay out of the new union (opting out); and Indian participation in the war-time government, but with defence under British control.

The Congress rejected the offer because it promised only dominion status in the future, gave no real power immediately and the opt-out clause opened the way to partition; Gandhi reportedly called it a 'post-dated cheque on a crashing bank'. The Muslim League rejected it because it did not explicitly accept Pakistan. The failure led to the Quit India Movement.
These initiatives attempted to address the transfer of power and political deadlock during the final years of colonial rule.

The Wavell Plan (June 1945), proposed by Viceroy Lord Wavell, offered to reconstitute the Executive Council with all members Indian except the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief, with equal representation of caste Hindus and Muslims. At the Simla Conference, Jinnah insisted that the League alone should nominate all Muslim members, which the Congress (whose president was Maulana Azad, a Muslim) refused, so the conference failed.

The Cabinet Mission (March-June 1946) - Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander - proposed a federal union with control over defence, foreign affairs and communications; provinces grouped into three sections (Group A Hindu-majority, Groups B and C in the north-west and east with Muslim majorities); a Constituent Assembly; and an interim government. The League accepted at first, then withdrew after a dispute over the grouping and called for 'Direct Action Day' (16 August 1946), which led to the Calcutta riots. The interim government under Nehru was formed in September 1946, and the League later joined it.
The Mountbatten Plan provided the immediate framework for partition and transfer of power in 1947.

In February 1947, British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced that Britain would leave India by June 1948. Lord Mountbatten became Viceroy in March 1947. Finding the situation deteriorating with communal riots, he announced the 3 June Plan (Mountbatten Plan): India would be partitioned into two dominions, India and Pakistan; the legislative assemblies of Punjab and Bengal would vote on partition of their provinces; a referendum would be held in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet; and princely states could join either dominion or remain independent.

The date of transfer was advanced to 15 August 1947. Boundary commissions under Sir Cyril Radcliffe drew the borders in Punjab and Bengal. Partition caused massive violence and the migration of about 10-15 million people, with perhaps up to a million deaths. Congress and the League accepted the plan as the only way to end the deadlock.
The Act legally provided for the creation of India and Pakistan and ended British parliamentary sovereignty over British India.

The Indian Independence Act was passed by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 based on the Mountbatten Plan. Its provisions: two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947; the end of British paramountcy over princely states; the Constituent Assemblies of each dominion would have full legislative power and could frame their constitutions; the British Crown would no longer be responsible for government; the office of Secretary of State for India was abolished; and each dominion would have a Governor-General.

Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of India and Jinnah of Pakistan. The princely states were integrated into India largely through the efforts of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon using the Instrument of Accession, though Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir posed problems. The Act ended British rule after nearly two centuries.

sections.title: From the Revolt of 1857 to Swadeshi

blocks.text:
The Revolt of 1857 was caused by a combination of political annexations, economic grievances, military discontent and social fears. Its suppression led to major changes in British rule.

The Indian National Congress later created an organised political platform. Moderates initially used constitutional methods, while Extremists called for stronger mobilisation.

The Partition of Bengal in 1905 produced the Swadeshi Movement, which connected boycott, indigenous production and national education with anti-colonial politics.

1857: causes included Dalhousie's annexations (Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh 1856), economic distress of peasants, artisans and taluqdars, fear of religious interference, the grievances of sepoys (low pay, overseas service, discrimination) and the greased cartridges. It began at Meerut (10 May 1857) and spread to Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bareilly, Bihar and central India, led by Bahadur Shah Zafar, Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal and Kunwar Singh. It failed due to lack of unity, planning and modern weapons, the loyalty of Punjab, Bengal and the south, the support of many princes for the British and superior British resources. It led to Crown rule (1858), the reorganisation of the army (more European troops, recruitment of 'martial races') and a policy of non-interference and alliance with princes and landlords.

Congress and the Moderates (1885-1905): the founding of the Congress followed earlier associations (the British Indian Association, Indian Association, Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, Madras Mahajan Sabha). The Moderates built national consciousness through the economic critique of colonialism (Naoroji, R. C. Dutt, Ranade), demands for constitutional reforms and civil rights, and constitutional methods. The Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Pal, Aurobindo) demanded swaraj and mass action.

Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi (1905-1908): Curzon's partition aimed to weaken Bengali nationalism and divide Hindus and Muslims. The Swadeshi movement used boycott, swadeshi enterprises, national education, samitis and cultural revival (Tagore). It spread nationalism to new groups and areas, but its limited appeal to Muslim peasants, the Surat split (1907) and repression led to its decline; some youth turned to revolutionary terrorism (the Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar; Khudiram Bose). The partition was annulled in 1911.

sections.title: Political Currents in the National Movement

blocks.text:
The Home Rule Movement revived demands for self-government. At the same time, communal political consciousness developed through organisations such as the Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha.

Left-wing politics grew through the Congress Socialist Party and Communist Party of India. Revolutionary nationalism was represented by figures such as Bhagat Singh and Surya Sen.

The INA and the RIN Mutiny formed important developments in the final phase of British rule.

Home Rule: Tilak's and Besant's Leagues (1916) mobilised opinion through propaganda and organisation, paving the way for the Lucknow Pact (1916) and the Montagu Declaration (1917), and preparing a new generation of activists for Gandhian politics. Communal politics: the Muslim League (1906) and separate electorates (1909), the Hindu Mahasabha and RSS, communal riots in the 1920s, and later the Lahore Resolution (1940) and two-nation theory led towards Partition. Historians (Bipan Chandra) argue that communalism was a modern phenomenon encouraged by colonial policy and middle-class competition.

The left: the CPI (1920/1925), trade unions and kisan sabhas, the CSP (1934), and leftist leaders like Nehru and Bose pushed Congress towards socialist and pro-peasant programmes. Revolutionaries: the Ghadar Party (1913), the HRA/HSRA (Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Kakori conspiracy 1925; Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh), and the Chittagong group of Surya Sen; they inspired youth though their methods differed from Gandhi's.

Final phase: the INA under Subhas Chandra Bose fought with Japan (Imphal-Kohima, 1944) and the INA trials (1945-1946) generated huge public support. The RIN Mutiny (February 1946) and strikes in the air force and army showed that Britain could no longer rely on Indian armed forces. Combined with economic exhaustion after the Second World War and the Labour government's attitude, these events made British withdrawal inevitable.

Gandhi brought non-violent mass mobilisation to the centre of the national movement. Non-Cooperation encouraged withdrawal from colonial institutions, while Civil Disobedience openly broke selected colonial laws.

The Quit India Movement of 1942 demanded immediate British withdrawal. Despite severe repression, it showed the depth of anti-colonial feeling.

These movements expanded nationalism beyond elite politics and involved wider sections of Indian society.

Gandhi's methods: satyagraha (non-violent resistance based on truth), non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting and constructive programmes (khadi, village industries, Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability, prohibition). His early campaigns in Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad (1917-1918) and the Rowlatt satyagraha (1919) established him as a mass leader. His use of simple symbols (spinning wheel, salt) and Indian languages connected with peasants and ordinary people.

Non-Cooperation and Khilafat (1920-1922): boycott of councils, courts, schools and foreign goods; national schools; the spread of nationalism to towns and villages; Hindu-Muslim unity; and withdrawal after Chauri Chaura. Civil Disobedience (1930-1934): Purna Swaraj, the Salt March, breaking of salt, forest and tax laws, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Round Table Conferences; wider participation of women, peasants and the frontier (Khudai Khidmatgars), though Muslim participation was lower. Quit India (1942): 'Do or Die', immediate arrest of leaders, spontaneous mass uprising, parallel governments and severe repression.

Evaluation: Gandhi made nationalism a mass movement and gave it a moral and non-violent character. Critics point to his sudden withdrawals of movements, his compromise with landlords and capitalists (according to Marxist historians), his religious idiom (which some argue alienated Muslims) and his conflict with Ambedkar over separate electorates (Poona Pact, 1932). Each movement nevertheless weakened British authority and widened the social base of nationalism.

The Simon Commission and Nehru Report formed part of debates over India's constitutional future. During the Second World War, the Cripps Mission failed to resolve the political deadlock.

The Wavell Plan and Cabinet Mission made further attempts to create an agreed transfer of power. Continuing disagreement eventually led to the Mountbatten Plan.

The Indian Independence Act of 1947 created India and Pakistan and formally ended British rule.

1919-1935: the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms (Government of India Act 1919) introduced dyarchy in the provinces. The all-white Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted, and the Nehru Report (1928) proposed an Indian constitution with dominion status and fundamental rights. The three Round Table Conferences (1930-1932) and the Communal Award (1932) led to the Government of India Act 1935, which provided for provincial autonomy and an all-India federation (never implemented). Congress ministries were formed in 1937 in most provinces but resigned in 1939 when India was taken into the war without consultation.

War years: the August Offer (1940) and the Cripps Mission (1942) failed; the Quit India movement followed. After the war, the Wavell Plan and Simla Conference (1945) failed over the League's claim to represent all Muslims; the elections of 1945-1946 showed the Congress dominant in general seats and the League in Muslim seats. The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) proposed a united India with groupings; disagreement and the League's Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) led to communal violence. An interim government and the Constituent Assembly (December 1946) were formed.

Independence and Partition: Attlee's announcement (February 1947), Mountbatten's 3 June Plan, and the Indian Independence Act (July 1947) created India and Pakistan on 14-15 August 1947. Partition led to massive violence and migration. The Constituent Assembly, chaired by Rajendra Prasad with Ambedkar as Chairman of the Drafting Committee, framed the Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950.
The Portuguese were the first major European maritime power to establish a lasting presence in India after the opening of the sea route around the Cape of Good Hope.

After Vasco da Gama's arrival at Calicut (1498), the Portuguese built their 'Estado da India'. Francisco de Almeida (1505-1509) pursued naval dominance and defeated a combined Egyptian-Gujarati fleet at Diu (1509). Afonso de Albuquerque (1509-1515) captured Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515), controlling key points of Indian Ocean trade; he encouraged Portuguese marriages with local women. Nino da Cunha acquired Diu and Bassein from Gujarat.

The Portuguese used the cartaz (pass) system and forced Asian traders to pay customs at their ports. They spread Catholicism (the Jesuit Francis Xavier; the Goa Inquisition from 1560), introduced tobacco, chilli, potato, maize, cashew and pineapple, and the printing press (1556). Their decline resulted from competition with the Dutch and English, religious intolerance, corruption, the small population of Portugal and its union with Spain (1580-1640). They lost Hooghly to the Mughals (1632) but held Goa, Daman and Diu until 1961.
The Dutch entered Indian Ocean commerce mainly for trade and established commercial centres, though they did not build a large territorial empire in India.

The Dutch East India Company (Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, VOC) was formed in 1602. Its main interest was the spice trade of the Indonesian islands; in India it sought textiles to exchange for spices. It established factories at Masulipatnam (1605), Pulicat (1610, its main base on the Coromandel coast, later Negapatnam), Surat (1616), Chinsura (Bengal, 1653), Kasimbazar, Patna, Balasore and Cochin (captured from the Portuguese, 1663).

The Dutch exported Indian textiles, indigo, saltpetre, raw silk and opium. Their power in India declined after the English defeated them at the Battle of Chinsura or Bidara (1759), and they concentrated on Indonesia. An Anglo-Dutch agreement (1667) had already given the Dutch the Indonesian islands while the English focused on India.
The French East India Company established settlements and competed with the English for political and commercial influence.

The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was founded in 1664 under Colbert, minister of Louis XIV; it was a state-controlled company. François Caron set up the first factory at Surat (1668); Masulipatnam followed (1669). François Martin founded Pondicherry (1674), which became the headquarters; other settlements were Chandernagore (Bengal, 1690), Mahe, Karaikal and Yanam.

Under Governor-General Joseph François Dupleix (1742-1754), the French began interfering in Indian politics to gain territory and revenue, using trained Indian soldiers (sepoys) and supporting rival claimants to thrones. This led to the Carnatic Wars with the English. The French were finally defeated at Wandiwash (1760) and lost Pondicherry (1761), though it was returned and remained French until 1954.
The English East India Company began as a trading corporation and gradually became a territorial and political power.

The English East India Company received a charter from Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600 for trade in the East. Captain William Hawkins visited Jahangir's court (1608); after the English defeated the Portuguese at Swally (1612), Jahangir allowed a factory at Surat (1613). Sir Thomas Roe, ambassador of James I, obtained further privileges (1615-1619). The Company acquired Madras (Fort St George, 1639-1640), Bombay (received from Charles II, who got it as dowry from Portugal, 1668) and Calcutta (founded by Job Charnock, 1690; Fort William, 1696).

The Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar's farman (1717) gave the Company duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for a yearly payment, which led to misuse of dastaks (passes) by Company servants. In the eighteenth century, the Company became a political and military power through wars in the Carnatic and Bengal, gradually transforming into a territorial ruler.
English and French competition in India became connected with wider European conflict and local Indian politics.

The English and French companies competed for trade in South India and in Bengal. Their rivalry was linked to European wars: the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-1748), the Seven Years' War (1756-1763) and later the American War of Independence and Napoleonic Wars. Both used the disputes of Indian rulers over succession to gain influence, supporting rival claimants in Hyderabad and the Carnatic.

The English won because of their stronger navy, better financial resources (Bengal's revenue after Plassey), the support of the British government, better commanders (Clive, Eyre Coote) and the recall of Dupleix (1754). The French company was state-controlled and poorly supported. The French continued to help Indian rulers (Haidar Ali, Tipu Sultan, the Marathas) against the English, but never recovered their power.
Hyderabad emerged as an important successor state as Mughal central authority weakened.

Hyderabad was founded as an autonomous state in 1724 by Mir Qamaruddin Khan Siddiqi, known as Chin Qilich Khan and Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, a powerful Mughal noble and viceroy of the Deccan. After defeating the Mughal governor at Shakar Kheda (1724), he ruled practically independently while acknowledging the Mughal emperor formally. His dynasty, the Asaf Jahis (Nizams), ruled until 1948.

Hyderabad faced pressure from the Marathas (who extracted chauth), the English and the French. After Nizam-ul-Mulk's death (1748), a succession dispute between Nasir Jang and Muzaffar Jang involved the English and French in the Second Carnatic War. The Nizam later signed the Subsidiary Alliance (1798) with Wellesley. Hyderabad was the largest princely state in India and was integrated into India in 1948 by 'Operation Polo'.
The Carnatic Wars were a series of conflicts involving English and French companies and Indian political powers. British success weakened French political influence.

First Carnatic War (1746-1748): part of the War of the Austrian Succession. The French under La Bourdonnais captured Madras (1746); Dupleix defeated the army of the Nawab of the Carnatic, Anwaruddin, at St Thome (Adyar, 1746), showing the superiority of trained European troops. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) restored Madras to the English.

Second Carnatic War (1749-1754): over succession disputes in Hyderabad (Nasir Jang vs Muzaffar Jang) and the Carnatic (Anwaruddin's son Muhammad Ali vs Chanda Sahib). The French supported Muzaffar Jang and Chanda Sahib; the English supported their rivals. Robert Clive's capture and defence of Arcot (1751) turned the war in the English favour; Muhammad Ali became Nawab. Dupleix was recalled in 1754. Third Carnatic War (1756-1763): part of the Seven Years' War. The French under Count de Lally lost to Sir Eyre Coote at Wandiwash (1760), and Pondicherry fell (1761). The Treaty of Paris (1763) returned Pondicherry but forbade French fortifications, ending French political ambitions in India.
Company power in Bengal expanded through military victory and political control, making Bengal a crucial base for British expansion.

Siraj-ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal (1756), opposed the English fortification of Calcutta, the misuse of dastaks and their sheltering of his enemies. He captured Calcutta (1756); the 'Black Hole' incident (the alleged death of English prisoners in a small room) was used for propaganda. Robert Clive recaptured Calcutta and conspired with Mir Jafar (the Nawab's commander), Jagat Seth (bankers) and others. At the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757), Mir Jafar's betrayal led to Siraj's defeat. Mir Jafar became Nawab and paid huge sums to the Company and its officers.

Mir Qasim (1760-1763), who replaced Mir Jafar, tried to assert independence, moving his capital to Monghyr and abolishing internal duties for everyone. He was defeated, and allied with Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II; their combined army lost at Buxar (22 October 1764). By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Shah Alam granted the Company the diwani (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. Bengal's wealth gave the Company resources for further expansion.
Mysore under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan became a major opponent of British expansion.

Haidar Ali, a soldier who rose to control the Wodeyar kingdom of Mysore (1761), built a modern army with French help. In the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-1769), he forced the English to sign the Treaty of Madras on his terms. In the Second (1780-1784), he defeated the English but died in 1782; his son Tipu Sultan concluded the Treaty of Mangalore (1784).

Tipu Sultan (1782-1799), the 'Tiger of Mysore', introduced a new calendar, coinage, weights and measures, promoted trade and industry, planted a 'Tree of Liberty' and joined the Jacobin Club in Seringapatam, and sought help from France and the Ottomans. He used iron-cased rockets in battle. In the Third War (1790-1792), Cornwallis allied with the Marathas and the Nizam and forced Tipu to cede half his territory (Treaty of Seringapatam). In the Fourth War (1799), Wellesley's forces stormed Seringapatam; Tipu died fighting. The Wodeyars were restored under a Subsidiary Alliance.
The Marathas were a major Indian power whose conflicts with the British ended in the expansion of Company supremacy.

The Maratha confederacy after Panipat (1761) was led by the Peshwa at Pune and great chiefs - the Gaekwad (Baroda), Holkar (Indore), Sindhia (Gwalior) and Bhonsle (Nagpur). The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-1782) arose from the English support for Raghunath Rao's claim to the Peshwaship; the Marathas, guided by Nana Phadnavis and Mahadji Sindhia, held their own, and the Treaty of Salbai (1782) restored the status quo.

After Nana Phadnavis's death (1800), internal conflict led Peshwa Baji Rao II to sign the Treaty of Bassein (1802), accepting a Subsidiary Alliance. This caused the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-1805), in which Wellesley and Lake defeated Sindhia and Bhonsle (battles of Assaye, Laswari). The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-1818) under Lord Hastings ended Maratha power: the Peshwa's territories were annexed, Baji Rao II was pensioned off at Bithur, and a small state at Satara was created for Shivaji's descendants.
The Sikh kingdom in Punjab remained an important power until Anglo-Sikh conflicts led to British annexation.

Ranjit Singh (1780-1839) united the Sikh misls, captured Lahore (1799) and Amritsar, and built a powerful kingdom including Kashmir, Multan and Peshawar. He modernised his army (the Fauj-i-Khas) with European officers, maintained friendly relations with the British (Treaty of Amritsar, 1809, fixing the Sutlej as the boundary) and obtained the Koh-i-Noor diamond.

After his death, instability, palace intrigues and the power of the army (Khalsa) led to wars with the British. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-1846; Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon) ended with the Treaty of Lahore, ceding territory (Jalandhar Doab; Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh). The Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-1849; Chillianwala, Gujrat) led Dalhousie to annex Punjab in 1849. The young Maharaja Duleep Singh was sent to England and the Koh-i-Noor was taken to Queen Victoria.
Awadh came increasingly under Company influence and was eventually annexed.

Awadh became an autonomous state under Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (1722). After Buxar (1764), Shuja-ud-Daulah became an ally of the Company, paying for British troops. The Nawabs' financial burden increased under Warren Hastings (who pressured the Begums of Awadh to give up their treasure) and Wellesley (1801 treaty, by which the Nawab ceded half his territory, including Rohilkhand and the Doab).

Awadh was known for its rich culture in Lucknow (the Bara Imambara, Lucknowi tehzeeb, Urdu poetry, music and dance). Dalhousie annexed it in February 1856 on grounds of 'misgovernment', exiling Nawab Wajid Ali Shah to Calcutta. The annexation angered taluqdars, soldiers (many sepoys came from Awadh) and common people, making Awadh a major centre of the 1857 revolt under Begum Hazrat Mahal.
Under the Subsidiary Alliance system, Indian rulers accepted British troops and political restrictions, reducing their independence.

Developed by Lord Wellesley (Governor-General, 1798-1805), though the French Dupleix had used similar ideas. Under it, an Indian ruler had to: accept a British army stationed in his territory and pay for it (in cash or by ceding territory); accept a British Resident at his court; not employ other Europeans without British approval; not make war or alliances with other states without British consent; and in return, the British would protect him from external and internal enemies.

The first to accept was the Nizam of Hyderabad (1798); others included Mysore (1799), Tanjore (1799), Awadh (1801), the Peshwa (1802), Bhonsle and Sindhia (1803). Effects: rulers lost independence, became financially burdened, often neglected administration, and many disbanded their armies, leaving soldiers unemployed. The British gained a large army paid for by Indian states, control over foreign affairs and an excuse to annex states that failed to pay.
The Doctrine of Lapse allowed the Company to annex certain states where it refused to recognise an adopted heir as successor.

Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General, 1848-1856) applied the Doctrine of Lapse: if a ruler of a dependent state died without a natural male heir, the state would 'lapse' to the Company, and adoption of an heir would not be recognised without permission. States annexed included Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (Chhattisgarh, 1852), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854).

Dalhousie also abolished titles and pensions, such as Nana Saheb's pension as the adopted son of Baji Rao II. The policy created deep resentment among Indian rulers and their subjects. Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, whose adopted son was not recognised, and Nana Saheb became important leaders of 1857. After 1857, Queen Victoria's Proclamation abandoned the Doctrine of Lapse and recognised the right of adoption.
The Dual System in Bengal divided formal authority and practical revenue power in a way that benefited the Company while weakening accountability.

After obtaining the diwani in 1765, Clive introduced the Dual System of Government in Bengal (1765-1772). The Company had the diwani (revenue collection and civil justice), while the Nawab retained the nizamat (police, criminal justice and administration). In practice, the Company appointed deputy diwans (Muhammad Reza Khan for Bengal, Shitab Rai for Bihar) to collect revenue, and also controlled the deputy nazim.

Thus the Company had power without responsibility, while the Nawab had responsibility without power. The result was misgovernment, oppressive revenue collection, corruption among Company servants and the ruin of Bengal's economy and artisans. The terrible Bengal famine of 1770 killed about a third of the population. Warren Hastings abolished the system in 1772, and the Company took direct charge of administration.
The Regulating Act was an early attempt by the British Parliament to supervise the East India Company's political activities in India.

The Regulating Act was passed by the British Parliament under Prime Minister Lord North in 1773, after the Company faced financial crisis and reports of corruption. It was the first step towards parliamentary control over the Company. The Governor of Bengal became the Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings was the first), with a council of four members, and the governors of Bombay and Madras were made subordinate to him in matters of war and peace.

A Supreme Court was established at Calcutta (1774) with a chief justice (Elijah Impey) and three judges. Company servants were prohibited from private trade and accepting bribes or gifts. The Court of Directors had to submit reports on revenue, civil and military affairs to the government. Defects: the Governor-General could be outvoted by his council; the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and the council was unclear; and the presidencies' subordination was ineffective. These defects led to the Act of 1781 and Pitt's India Act.
Pitt's India Act increased British government control over the Company's political administration.

Pitt's India Act (1784), passed under Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger, created a dual system of control: the Court of Directors managed commercial affairs, while a Board of Control (six members, including the Chancellor of the Exchequer and a Secretary of State) supervised civil, military and revenue affairs. The Company's territories in India were called 'British possessions in India' for the first time.

The Governor-General's council was reduced to three members; the Governor-General was given control over Bombay and Madras in matters of war, revenue and diplomacy. The Act of 1786 allowed Cornwallis to override his council and to be also Commander-in-Chief. The system of dual control lasted until 1858, when the Crown took over directly.
The Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853 progressively altered Company privileges, administration and the relationship between trade and government.

Charter Act of 1793: renewed the Company's charter and trade monopoly for twenty years; strengthened the powers of the Governor-General over the council and presidencies; salaries of the Board of Control were paid from Indian revenues. Charter Act of 1813: ended the Company's trade monopoly in India (except for tea and trade with China); allowed Christian missionaries to enter India; and allocated one lakh rupees annually for education - the first commitment to education.

Charter Act of 1833: ended the Company's commercial functions entirely, making it a purely administrative body; the Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor-General of India (William Bentinck was the first), with full legislative powers for the whole country; a law member (Macaulay) was added to the council; and it declared that no Indian would be denied office due to religion, birth or colour. Charter Act of 1853: separated the legislative and executive functions of the council, created a legislative council, introduced open competition for the civil service (the Indian Civil Service), and did not renew the charter for a fixed period, foreshadowing the end of Company rule.
Political annexation, economic grievances, military discontent and social and religious anxieties contributed to the revolt.

Political causes: aggressive annexations (Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh), the humiliation of the Mughal emperor (Dalhousie and Canning announced that Bahadur Shah's successors would lose the title and palace), and the loss of power and pensions of rulers and nobles. Economic causes: high land revenue and the loss of land by peasants and taluqdars (especially in Awadh under the Summary Settlement, 1856); ruin of artisans by British imports; unemployment of soldiers and officials of annexed states.

Social and religious causes: fear of Christian conversion (missionary activities, the Religious Disabilities Act 1850, which allowed converts to inherit), social reforms (abolition of sati, Widow Remarriage Act 1856), Western education and railways and telegraphs seen as threats to caste and religion, and British racial arrogance. Military causes: low pay and limited promotion for Indian sepoys; withdrawal of allowances (bhatta) for service outside their areas; the General Service Enlistment Act (1856); the British army's reverses in the Crimean and Afghan wars; and the immediate cause, the greased cartridges of the new Enfield rifle, which had to be bitten open and were rumoured to contain cow and pig fat.
The Revolt had different regional forms and involved soldiers, rulers and sections of the population. Historians debate how it should be characterised.

Interpretations: (1) a 'sepoy mutiny', according to British officials like John Seeley and some Indian contemporaries; (2) a 'national war of independence', according to V. D. Savarkar ('The Indian War of Independence of 1857', 1909); (3) a feudal reaction by dispossessed rulers and landlords trying to restore the old order, according to some historians (R. C. Majumdar argued it was 'neither first, nor national, nor war of independence'); (4) a 'conspiracy' of Muslims to restore Mughal rule, an old British view now rejected; (5) a combination of military revolt and popular uprising, as argued by S. N. Sen and Eric Stokes, who showed the role of peasants.

Recent historians (Rudrangshu Mukherjee on Awadh, Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern school) emphasise the participation of peasants and the rural population, especially in Awadh and western Bihar, where the revolt became a widespread civil rebellion, with Hindus and Muslims fighting together. Its character varied by region. Most agree it was the most serious challenge to British rule in the nineteenth century, whatever label is used.
Limited coordination, uneven regional participation, British military resources and other weaknesses contributed to its defeat.

Reasons for failure: (1) limited spread - the revolt was concentrated in north and central India; Punjab, Bengal, the south and most of western India remained quiet; (2) many rulers (Sindhia, Holkar, the Nizam, the Sikh chiefs, the Rana of Nepal) supported the British; (3) lack of central leadership, coordination and common programme - leaders fought for local aims; Bahadur Shah was old and weak; (4) inferior arms and organisation against British rifles, artillery and the telegraph, which allowed rapid communication; (5) British resources from the empire, including troops from Britain and those diverted from China.

In addition, the educated middle class, merchants and moneylenders mostly did not support the revolt, and British commanders such as Colin Campbell, Hugh Rose, Henry Havelock and John Nicholson were able. Delhi was recaptured in September 1857, Lucknow and Kanpur in 1858, and Rani Lakshmibai died fighting at Gwalior (June 1858). Tantia Tope was captured and hanged (1859). The British took brutal revenge, including mass executions.
Company rule ended and the British Crown assumed direct authority. Colonial military and administrative policies were reorganised.

The Government of India Act 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown. A Secretary of State for India (with a council of fifteen members) in London became responsible for Indian affairs, and the Governor-General became the Viceroy (Canning was the first). Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858) announced the end of annexations, respect for treaties with princes and their right to adopt heirs, non-interference in religion, equal protection of the law and a general amnesty.

Military reorganisation: the ratio of European to Indian soldiers was increased; artillery was kept in European hands; recruitment shifted to 'martial races' (Sikhs, Gurkhas, Pathans) from areas loyal in 1857, and regiments were mixed to prevent unity ('divide and rule'). Other effects: the British became allies of princes and landlords; social reforms slowed; racial distance between rulers and ruled widened; and the policy of divide and rule between Hindus and Muslims began. The Mughal dynasty ended with Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile to Rangoon.

sections.title: Advent of European Powers and Carnatic Wars

blocks.text:
Portuguese, Dutch, French and English commercial powers entered India through maritime trade. Over time, European rivalry became linked with Indian regional politics.

The Anglo-French rivalry was especially important in the Carnatic Wars. Both companies supported competing Indian political interests, but British victories weakened French political ambitions.

These conflicts helped create the conditions for the English East India Company's transformation from merchant organisation into territorial power.

European arrival: the Portuguese (1498) built a maritime empire based on Goa and the cartaz system; the Dutch (VOC, 1602) concentrated on spices and textiles, with bases at Pulicat and Chinsura, and were displaced in India after Bidara (1759); the English (1600) established Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta and gained privileges from the Mughals; the French (1664) established Pondicherry and Chandernagore. The Danes also had settlements (Tranquebar, Serampore).

Carnatic Wars: in the First (1746-1748), the French took Madras and Dupleix defeated the Nawab, showing the strength of European-trained troops; in the Second (1749-1754), the companies backed rival claimants in Hyderabad and the Carnatic, and Clive's seizure of Arcot (1751) led to English success; in the Third (1756-1763), Eyre Coote defeated Lally at Wandiwash (1760) and Pondicherry fell.

Reasons for English success: naval superiority, financial strength (especially Bengal's revenues after Plassey), the private character and commercial efficiency of the English company compared with the state-controlled French company, consistent support from the British government, able leaders, and Dupleix's recall. The Carnatic Wars taught the English how to use Indian political divisions and trained sepoys to gain power - lessons applied in Bengal.

sections.title: Expansion and Consolidation of British Rule

blocks.text:
British power expanded first strongly in Bengal and later through wars, alliances and annexations involving Mysore, the Marathas, Punjab and Awadh.

This was not a single continuous conquest. Different regions resisted British expansion and were incorporated under different circumstances.

By the mid-nineteenth century, the East India Company had become the dominant territorial power over much of the subcontinent.

Bengal: Plassey (1757) made the Company the kingmaker in Bengal; Buxar (1764) and the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave it the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. Bengal's resources financed later wars. Mysore: four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-1799) against Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, ending with Tipu's death and a subsidiary alliance with the restored Wodeyars. Marathas: three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775-1782, 1803-1805, 1817-1818); internal divisions after Nana Phadnavis's death and the Treaty of Bassein led to the end of Maratha power.

Punjab: after Ranjit Singh's death (1839), instability led to two Anglo-Sikh wars and annexation in 1849. Awadh: subjected to subsidiary treaties and territorial cessions (1801) and annexed in 1856. Other annexations: Sindh (1843, by Charles Napier - 'Peccavi'), Burma (wars of 1824-1826 and 1852, annexation of Lower Burma; full annexation 1885), and states taken under the Doctrine of Lapse.

Methods: wars, diplomacy, the Subsidiary Alliance, the Doctrine of Lapse, annexation on grounds of misgovernment, and exploiting rivalries among Indian powers. Reasons for success: military superiority (discipline, artillery, sepoy armies), financial resources, naval power, the lack of unity among Indian states and able leaders such as Clive, Hastings, Cornwallis, Wellesley, Hastings (Moira) and Dalhousie. By 1857, the Company ruled or controlled almost all of India.

The Subsidiary Alliance restricted the independence of Indian rulers by placing them within a British-controlled military and diplomatic system. The Doctrine of Lapse became another instrument of annexation.

Administrative changes included the Dual System in Bengal and parliamentary measures such as the Regulating Act of 1773, Pitt's India Act of 1784 and Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853.

These measures gradually increased British state supervision and reshaped Company government.

Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley): Indian rulers accepted British troops, a Resident, and British control over foreign relations, paying subsidies or ceding territory. It turned states into dependencies (Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh, the Peshwa) and gave the British a large army at Indian expense. Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie): states without natural heirs were annexed (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur). Annexation on grounds of misgovernment (Awadh, 1856) completed British expansion.

Administrative changes: Clive's Dual System (1765-1772) gave the Company revenue power without responsibility, leading to misrule and the 1770 famine. The Regulating Act (1773) created the Governor-General of Bengal and the Supreme Court at Calcutta and began parliamentary control. Pitt's India Act (1784) set up the Board of Control. Charter Acts: 1793 (renewal), 1813 (end of trade monopoly except tea and China trade, entry of missionaries, education grant), 1833 (end of commercial functions, Governor-General of India, centralised legislation, law commission under Macaulay), 1853 (separate legislative council, open competition for civil service).

Other reforms: Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement (1793), civil service and judicial reforms (the Cornwallis Code); Bentinck's social reforms (abolition of sati, 1829) and English education (Macaulay's Minute, 1835); Dalhousie's railways (1853), telegraph and postal reforms. These changes centralised authority and prepared the structure of later colonial government.

The Revolt of 1857 resulted from accumulated political, military, economic and social grievances. It spread across important parts of northern and central India, though participation varied greatly by region.

Its nature remains debated because it combined a sepoy uprising with broader resistance involving rulers and civilian groups in some areas. Lack of unified leadership and uneven geographical support helped the British suppress it.

The revolt ended Company rule. In 1858 the British Crown took direct control, and military and administrative policies were reorganised.

Causes: political (annexations, insult to the Mughals), economic (land revenue, ruin of crafts, loss of taluqdars' rights), social and religious (fear of conversion and interference), and military (sepoy grievances and greased cartridges). Course: Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore (29 March 1857); the outbreak at Meerut (10 May) and the march to Delhi; risings at Kanpur (Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh), Bareilly (Khan Bahadur Khan) and Faizabad (Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah). The British recaptured Delhi in September 1857 and other centres in 1858.

Nature: interpretations range from 'sepoy mutiny' (British view) to 'first war of independence' (Savarkar), a feudal reaction, or a popular revolt with peasant participation (Stokes, Mukherjee, Guha). The best view is that it began as a military mutiny but became a widespread popular rebellion in some regions, with Hindu-Muslim unity and anti-British feeling, though not nationalism in the modern sense.

Failure and consequences: limited geographical spread, lack of unified leadership and plan, the loyalty of many princes and the educated class, and superior British resources led to defeat. The Government of India Act 1858 transferred power to the Crown; Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised no annexations and religious non-interference; the army was reorganised on 'divide and rule' lines; and the British became cautious about social reforms and allied with princes and landlords. The revolt left a legacy that inspired later nationalists.
The Middle Ages cover the long period between the ancient Roman world and the Renaissance. The syllabus studies political, social, economic and religious transformation from about 300 to 1500.

The term 'Middle Ages' (medium aevum) was coined by Renaissance humanists who saw the period between classical antiquity and their own revival of learning as a 'dark' middle period. Modern historians reject the idea of a 'Dark Age' and see the period as one of creativity and change. It is usually divided into the Early Middle Ages (c. 300/500-1000), the High or Central Middle Ages (c. 1000-1300) and the Late Middle Ages (c. 1300-1500).

Key themes include the transformation of the Roman world, the rise of Christianity and the Church, the barbarian kingdoms, the Carolingian empire, feudalism and manorialism, the revival of trade and towns, the Crusades, universities, and the crises of the fourteenth century. The period ended with the Renaissance, the fall of Constantinople (1453), the printing press and the voyages of discovery (1492).

sections.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

blocks.text: The western imperial structure weakened through political, military and economic pressures while new kingdoms emerged in former Roman territories.

The traditional date for the fall of the Western Empire is 476 CE, when the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople. Causes discussed by historians include: political instability and civil wars; the division of the empire (395 CE, after Theodosius); economic problems (heavy taxation, inflation, decline of trade); dependence on Germanic soldiers; pressure from the Huns, which pushed Goths and others into the empire; and military defeats such as Adrianople (378), the sack of Rome by Alaric's Visigoths (410) and the Vandals (455).

Edward Gibbon ('The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire', 1776-1788) blamed Christianity and the loss of civic virtue. Modern historians such as Peter Brown speak of 'transformation' in 'Late Antiquity' rather than fall, emphasising continuities in law, language, the Church and urban life, while others (Bryan Ward-Perkins) stress real economic decline and violence.
Population movements and the formation of new group identities shaped the early medieval political map.

Migration (the Völkerwanderung, or 'migration period') from the fourth to sixth centuries brought Goths, Vandals, Franks, Burgundians, Angles, Saxons, Lombards and others into Roman territory. The arrival of the Huns from the steppes around 370 CE pushed many groups westward.

Ethnogenesis means the formation of an ethnic identity. Historians such as Herwig Wolfram and Patrick Geary argue that 'barbarian' peoples were not ancient, fixed tribes but new groups formed during the migrations by combining various peoples under successful leaders and around shared traditions, laws and myths. For example, the Goths included people of different origins. Identities were flexible and politically constructed, a view that challenges older nationalist histories.
New kingdoms developed in western Europe after Roman imperial authority declined.

Major successor kingdoms: the Visigoths in Spain (capital Toledo), the Ostrogoths in Italy under Theodoric (493-526), the Vandals in North Africa (Carthage), the Burgundians in eastern Gaul, the Franks in Gaul under Clovis (481-511) of the Merovingian dynasty, who converted to Catholic Christianity (c. 496), the Anglo-Saxons in England, and later the Lombards in Italy (568).

These kingdoms combined Germanic traditions (warrior bands, kingship based on military leadership, customary law such as the Salic Law of the Franks) with Roman institutions (Latin, Roman law for Roman subjects, bishops and the Church, cities). Many rulers were initially Arian Christians, which created tension with Catholic subjects. The Frankish kingdom, being Catholic, became the most successful.
Roman imperial institutions survived in the East, later commonly called the Byzantine Empire.

The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, with its capital at Constantinople, survived until 1453. It was Greek-speaking, Christian (Orthodox), and governed by an emperor considered God's representative on earth, with an elaborate bureaucracy, a professional army and strong fortifications (the Theodosian Walls). Its economy was based on trade and a stable gold currency (the solidus or bezant).

Justinian I (527-565) reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of Spain, compiled the Corpus Juris Civilis and built Hagia Sophia. Later the empire lost territory to the Persians, Arabs (Syria, Egypt, North Africa in the seventh century) and Slavs, and was weakened by the iconoclasm controversy (726-843) and the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204). The Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople in 1453. Byzantium preserved Greek learning and influenced Russia and the Slavic world.
The Church became a major institution during the transition from Antiquity to the Middle Ages.

After Constantine and Theodosius, the Church became the most important institution in western Europe. It was organised in dioceses under bishops, with the Bishop of Rome (the Pope) claiming leadership as successor of St Peter. Pope Leo I (440-461) asserted papal primacy and Pope Gregory I (590-604) organised papal estates, sent missionaries to England (Augustine of Canterbury, 597) and strengthened the papacy.

Church Fathers such as St Augustine of Hippo ('City of God', 'Confessions'), St Jerome (Latin Vulgate Bible) and St Ambrose shaped Christian doctrine. The Church preserved literacy, Latin and classical learning through its clergy and monasteries, converted the barbarian peoples, provided social services, and gave legitimacy to kings. It also became a major landowner.
The relationship between secular rulers and the papacy became a major issue in medieval European politics.

Pope Gelasius I (494) formulated the 'two swords' theory: spiritual authority belonged to the Church and temporal authority to the emperor, but the spiritual was superior. The papacy allied with the Franks: Pepin the Short was anointed king (751-754) and gave the Pope lands in central Italy (the 'Donation of Pepin', basis of the Papal States); Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800. Otto I was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962.

The conflict reached its height in the Investiture Controversy (1075-1122) over who should appoint bishops: Pope Gregory VII excommunicated Emperor Henry IV, who did penance at Canossa (1077). The Concordat of Worms (1122) was a compromise. Later conflicts involved Frederick Barbarossa and Frederick II against the popes, and Boniface VIII against Philip IV of France ('Unam Sanctam', 1302, claiming papal supremacy). The relationship shaped ideas of church-state separation.
Monastic communities organised religious life around discipline, prayer and communal living and became important centres of learning and landholding.

Christian monasticism began in Egypt with hermits like St Anthony and communal monasteries under Pachomius. In the West, St Benedict of Nursia founded Monte Cassino (c. 529) and wrote the Rule of St Benedict, prescribing a balanced life of prayer (the divine office), manual labour and study under an abbot, with vows of poverty, chastity and obedience ('Ora et labora' - pray and work). Irish monks (St Columba, Columbanus) spread Christianity and learning.

Monasteries copied manuscripts in their scriptoria, preserving classical and Christian texts; ran schools; cleared forests and developed agriculture; provided hospitality, charity and medical care; and became major landowners. Reform movements arose when monasteries became wealthy and lax: Cluny (910), the Cistercians (Citeaux, 1098; St Bernard of Clairvaux), and later the mendicant (begging) friars - Franciscans (St Francis of Assisi, 1209) and Dominicans (St Dominic, 1216).
Arab conquests and the establishment of Islam transformed the Mediterranean and neighbouring regions.

After the Prophet Muhammad's death (632), the Arabs under the caliphs conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt and Persia within twenty years, then North Africa, and Spain (from 711), until they were stopped by Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours/Poitiers (732). The Umayyad caliphate (Damascus, 661-750) was followed by the Abbasids (Baghdad, 750-1258); an Umayyad emirate (later caliphate) continued in Córdoba, Spain.

The Belgian historian Henri Pirenne ('Mohammed and Charlemagne', 1937) argued that the Arab conquests, rather than the barbarian invasions, ended the unity of the Mediterranean world and its trade, turning western Europe inward towards an agrarian economy: 'Without Muhammad, Charlemagne would be inconceivable.' Later archaeology modified his thesis, showing trade continued. Islamic civilisation preserved and developed Greek philosophy, mathematics, medicine and astronomy, which later reached Europe through Spain and Sicily.
Power in the Frankish world was strongly connected with military leadership and control of land.

In the Frankish kingdoms, power depended on military force and land. The Merovingian kings (from Clovis) granted land to their warriors and nobles, weakening royal power; real power passed to the 'mayors of the palace'. Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, defeated the Arabs at Tours (732) and rewarded his followers with land (often taken from the Church) in exchange for military service, especially as mounted warriors.

Aristocratic families controlled large estates worked by dependent peasants and slaves, built followings of armed men (vassals) bound by oaths of loyalty, and competed for royal favour, offices and land. Historians debate how far this produced 'feudalism' - the system of lords, vassals and fiefs - which historians such as Susan Reynolds ('Fiefs and Vassals', 1994) argue was much less systematic than once believed.
Early medieval exchange included local and long-distance trade as well as gift-giving within political and social relationships.

Early medieval exchange included local markets, regional trade and long-distance trade in luxury goods (silk, spices, slaves, furs, amber) through Mediterranean, North Sea and Baltic routes. Emporia (trading towns) such as Dorestad (Netherlands), Quentovic, Hamwic (Southampton) and Hedeby (Denmark) flourished in the seventh to ninth centuries. Vikings combined raiding with trade from the Baltic to Byzantium and the Caliphate. Charlemagne introduced the silver penny (denier).

Gift exchange was central to social and political relationships: kings gave land, treasure, weapons and feasts to followers to secure loyalty, and received gifts in return; diplomatic gifts were exchanged between rulers (Harun al-Rashid's elephant for Charlemagne). Anthropologist Marcel Mauss's 'The Gift' (1925) showed that gifts create obligations. Historians such as Philip Grierson and Georges Duby emphasised the importance of gift-giving in the early medieval economy alongside commerce.
The Carolingians created a major political power in western Europe, especially under Charlemagne.

Pepin the Short, son of Charles Martel, deposed the last Merovingian king and became king of the Franks (751), with papal approval, founding the Carolingian dynasty. His son Charlemagne (Charles the Great, r. 768-814) conquered the Lombard kingdom in Italy (774), the Saxons (after brutal wars, forcing their conversion), Bavaria and the Avars, and fought the Muslims in Spain (the 'Song of Roland' is based on the battle of Roncesvalles, 778). His empire covered most of western and central Europe, with Aachen as capital.

He was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800. He governed through counts, inspected by royal agents (missi dominici), and issued capitularies (decrees). The 'Carolingian Renaissance' revived learning, with the scholar Alcuin of York at his palace school, the reform of the Church, the copying of manuscripts and the new Carolingian minuscule script.
Charlemagne's empire influenced later ideas of kingship, empire and Christian political order.

Charlemagne's empire was divided among his grandsons by the Treaty of Verdun (843) into West Francia (the origin of France), East Francia (the origin of Germany) and Middle Francia (Lotharingia, between them). Viking, Magyar and Muslim raids and weak rulers caused the decline of royal power, and local lords became stronger.

His legacy: the idea of a Christian empire allied with the papacy, revived by Otto I as the Holy Roman Empire (962-1806); the Carolingian Renaissance's preservation of classical texts (most surviving Latin classics come from Carolingian copies) and its script, which is the basis of modern lower-case letters; the model of a Christian king ruling with the Church; and the foundation of the later states of France and Germany. Charlemagne is sometimes called the 'Father of Europe'.
The development of England involved political consolidation and the growth of royal institutions.

After the Romans left Britain (c. 410), Anglo-Saxon kingdoms formed - the 'Heptarchy' of Northumbria, Mercia, Wessex, East Anglia, Essex, Sussex and Kent. Christianity spread through Augustine's mission (597) and Irish monks; the Venerable Bede wrote the 'Ecclesiastical History of the English People' (731). Viking invasions from the late eighth century led to the Danelaw, but Alfred the Great of Wessex (871-899) resisted the Danes, built fortified towns (burhs), promoted learning in English and laid foundations for a unified kingdom achieved by his successors (Athelstan, 927).

The Norman Conquest (1066), when William the Conqueror defeated Harold at Hastings, introduced Norman feudalism, French culture, castles, the Domesday Book (1086, a survey of land and resources) and a strong monarchy. Henry II (1154-1189) developed common law and royal courts. King John was forced to accept the Magna Carta (1215), which limited royal power. Parliament developed in the thirteenth century (Simon de Montfort's parliament, 1265; Edward I's 'Model Parliament', 1295).
Between 1000 and 1300 Europe experienced population growth and increased agricultural production.

Europe's population may have doubled or tripled between 1000 and 1300, from perhaps 35-40 million to about 70-80 million. Causes included the end of Viking, Magyar and Muslim invasions, a warmer climate (the 'Medieval Warm Period'), and agricultural improvements: the heavy wheeled plough (carruca) for the heavy soils of northern Europe; the horse collar and horseshoes, allowing horses to plough; the three-field rotation system (one field in winter crops, one in spring crops, one fallow), which increased production; and water mills and windmills.

Peasants cleared forests, drained marshes (in Flanders and the Netherlands) and colonised new lands, especially the German eastward expansion (Ostsiedlung). Increased food production supported population growth, the growth of towns and trade, and the expansion of Europe in the Crusades and Reconquista.
Medieval lordship connected warrior elites, landholding and peasant production, though actual social relations were more complex than idealised images.

The idealised medieval view divided society into three orders: those who pray (oratores - clergy), those who fight (bellatores - knights and nobles) and those who work (laboratores - peasants), as described by Bishop Adalbero of Laon (c. 1020). Knights were mounted warriors bound to lords by homage and fealty, receiving fiefs (land) in return for military service. Chivalry developed as a code of conduct emphasising bravery, loyalty, piety and protection of the weak, influenced by the Church and courtly literature.

Most peasants lived on manors controlled by lords. Serfs were bound to the land and owed labour services (working on the lord's demesne), dues in kind or cash, and payments for using the lord's mill, oven and press (banalities); they were subject to the lord's court. Free peasants paid rent. Peasants' lives were hard, but they had customary rights. Historians emphasise that real social relations varied greatly across regions and over time.
The papacy increased its institutional claims and political influence during the Central Middle Ages.

The Gregorian Reform (eleventh century), named after Pope Gregory VII (1073-1085), aimed to free the Church from lay control, end simony (buying of church offices) and enforce clerical celibacy. Gregory's 'Dictatus Papae' claimed that the Pope could depose emperors. The College of Cardinals was given the right to elect popes (1059). The Investiture Controversy followed.

The papacy reached its height under Innocent III (1198-1216), who intervened in the affairs of England (forcing King John to become his vassal), France and the Holy Roman Empire, launched the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathar heretics, and held the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), which defined doctrine (transubstantiation) and required annual confession. The papacy developed a bureaucracy, canon law, taxation and the Inquisition (from 1231). Its claims declined after Boniface VIII's conflict with Philip IV.
The Crusades were religiously justified military expeditions that created prolonged interaction and conflict between western Christians and the eastern Mediterranean.

Pope Urban II called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont (1095), after the Byzantine emperor Alexios I asked for help against the Seljuk Turks, who had defeated the Byzantines at Manzikert (1071). Crusaders were promised remission of sins. The First Crusade (1096-1099) captured Jerusalem (1099) with great massacres and established Crusader states: Jerusalem, Edessa, Antioch and Tripoli. Military orders (Templars, Hospitallers) were formed.

Later crusades: the Second (1147-1149) failed after the fall of Edessa; Saladin recaptured Jerusalem (1187) after the battle of Hattin; the Third Crusade (1189-1192) of Richard the Lionheart, Philip II and Frederick Barbarossa won coastal cities but not Jerusalem; the Fourth (1202-1204) sacked Constantinople. The last Crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291. Effects: increased trade with the East (benefiting Venice and Genoa), cultural contact, strengthening of papal and royal power, persecution of Jews, deepening of the split between the Latin and Orthodox churches and lasting hostility between Christians and Muslims.
Expansion of trade, transport and market activity contributed to the growth of a more commercial medieval economy.

Robert S. Lopez ('The Commercial Revolution of the Middle Ages, 950-1350') described the transformation of the European economy. Italian cities (Venice, Genoa, Pisa) dominated Mediterranean trade with the Byzantine and Islamic worlds, importing spices, silk and luxury goods. In the north, Flanders produced woollen cloth from English wool, and the Hanseatic League (from the thirteenth century), a confederation of German towns such as Lübeck and Hamburg, controlled Baltic and North Sea trade.

The Champagne fairs in France connected Italian and northern merchants. New business techniques included partnerships (commenda), bills of exchange, banking (the Medici, Bardi and Peruzzi of Florence), double-entry bookkeeping, insurance and new gold coins (the Florentine florin, 1252, and the Venetian ducat). Improvements in roads, ships and navigation (the compass) helped, and the countryside became more commercialised as peasants paid money rents and sold produce in towns.
Medieval universities developed as organised centres of advanced learning.

Universities (universitas, meaning a guild or corporation) developed from cathedral schools in the twelfth century. Bologna (c. 1088) was famous for law, organised by students; Paris (c. 1150-1200) for theology, organised by masters; and Oxford (c. 1167) and Cambridge (1209) followed. Others included Salerno (medicine), Montpellier, Padua and Salamanca. By 1500 there were about eighty universities.

Students studied the seven liberal arts - the trivium (grammar, rhetoric, logic) and quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music) - before higher faculties of theology, law and medicine. Teaching used lectures and disputations in Latin. Scholasticism tried to reconcile faith and reason using Aristotle's works (reintroduced through Arabic translations and commentaries of Avicenna and Averroes); key scholars were Peter Abelard ('Sic et Non') and Thomas Aquinas ('Summa Theologica'). Universities trained clergy, lawyers, doctors and officials.
The growth of towns transformed trade, occupations and social organisation in medieval Europe.

Towns grew from the eleventh century around castles, monasteries, old Roman sites, river crossings and markets, due to population growth, agricultural surplus and trade. Towns obtained charters from lords or kings granting rights of self-government, markets and freedom for inhabitants ('town air makes free' - a serf who lived in a town for a year and a day became free). Merchants and craftsmen formed guilds that regulated prices, quality, training (apprentice, journeyman, master) and protected members.

Major urban centres included Venice, Florence, Milan, Paris, London, Bruges, Ghent and Cologne. Towns created a new social group, the burghers or bourgeoisie, and led to conflicts with lords and between rich patricians and poorer artisans (the Ciompi revolt in Florence, 1378). Towns were centres of trade, crafts, education, cathedral-building (Gothic architecture) and new religious movements, and they laid the basis of modern urban society.
The fourteenth and fifteenth centuries were marked by war, famine, disease and demographic and economic contraction in many regions.

The fourteenth century saw a series of disasters: the Great Famine (1315-1317) caused by cold, wet weather (the beginning of the 'Little Ice Age'), the Black Death (1347-1351), a plague brought from Central Asia via the Black Sea to Italy, which killed about one-third to one-half of Europe's population, and recurrent plagues afterwards. The Hundred Years' War between England and France (1337-1453), with battles such as Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) and Joan of Arc's role (1429-1431), caused devastation.

Consequences: labour shortages raised wages and weakened serfdom; peasants revolted (the Jacquerie in France, 1358; the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381 under Wat Tyler against the poll tax); towns saw workers' revolts; Jews were persecuted as scapegoats; religious anxiety grew (flagellants); and the Church's prestige declined. Some historians see the crisis as a turning point that destroyed the medieval order and prepared the way for the Renaissance and new economic systems.
The Great Schism divided papal allegiance and contributed to a crisis of authority within the western Church.

The 'Babylonian Captivity' (1309-1377): after the conflict between Boniface VIII and Philip IV, the papacy moved to Avignon in France, where seven French popes lived under French influence. When Pope Gregory XI returned to Rome (1377), the subsequent election in 1378 led to two rival popes - Urban VI in Rome and Clement VII in Avignon. This Great Western Schism (1378-1417) divided Europe: France, Scotland and others supported Avignon, England and the Holy Roman Empire supported Rome. In 1409, the Council of Pisa added a third pope.

The conciliar movement held that a general council of the Church had authority over the Pope. The Council of Constance (1414-1418) ended the schism by deposing or accepting the resignation of the rival popes and electing Martin V; it also condemned and burned the Czech reformer Jan Hus. The Schism damaged papal prestige and encouraged critics such as John Wycliffe in England and Hus, foreshadowing the Reformation.
Humanism developed in the later Middle Ages and contributed to intellectual changes associated with the transition toward the Renaissance.

Humanism was an intellectual movement that emphasised the study of classical Latin and Greek literature (the studia humanitatis - grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy) and the dignity and potential of human beings. It began in fourteenth-century Italy with Francesco Petrarch (1304-1374), the 'father of humanism', who searched for classical manuscripts and wrote in Latin and Italian, and Giovanni Boccaccio ('Decameron'). Dante Alighieri's 'Divine Comedy' (early fourteenth century) is often seen as a bridge.

Later humanists included Coluccio Salutati and Leonardo Bruni (civic humanism in Florence), Lorenzo Valla (who proved that the 'Donation of Constantine' was a forgery), and the revival of Greek after Byzantine scholars came to Italy (Manuel Chrysoloras; the Council of Florence, 1439; the fall of Constantinople, 1453). The invention of printing by Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1450) spread humanist ideas. Humanism led to the Renaissance and influenced the Reformation (Erasmus).

sections.title: Early Middle Ages and the End of Rome

blocks.text:
The Early Middle Ages developed out of the transformation of the Roman world. Western imperial authority disappeared, but Roman culture and institutions did not simply vanish. New kingdoms emerged through migration, warfare and ethnogenesis.

The Eastern Roman Empire survived, while Christianity became increasingly important in western society. Church organisation, monasticism and relations between emperor and pope shaped medieval institutions.

The rise of Islam and Arab conquests also transformed the wider Mediterranean world.
