Transformation of the Roman world: the Western Empire faced political instability, economic difficulties and pressure from migrating peoples (Goths, Vandals, Franks, Anglo-Saxons), culminating in the deposition of Romulus Augustulus (476). Historians debate 'fall' (Gibbon, Ward-Perkins) versus 'transformation' (Peter Brown's Late Antiquity). Ethnogenesis theory argues that barbarian peoples formed new identities during migration. Barbarian kingdoms (Visigoths, Ostrogoths, Vandals, Franks, Lombards, Anglo-Saxons) combined Germanic and Roman traditions; Clovis's Catholic conversion made the Franks dominant.

Eastern Roman Empire: survived with its capital at Constantinople, a centralised state and Orthodox Christianity; Justinian's reconquests, legal code and Hagia Sophia; later losses to the Arabs. Church and monasticism: the papacy (Leo I, Gregory I) grew in authority; the theory of two swords (Gelasius); Benedictine monasticism preserved learning and developed agriculture; Irish and Anglo-Saxon missionaries converted northern Europe. The alliance of popes and Frankish kings (Pepin, Charlemagne) shaped medieval politics.

Islam: the Arab conquests (seventh-eighth centuries) took the southern and eastern Mediterranean and Spain, stopped at Tours (732). Pirenne argued this divided the Mediterranean and shifted Europe's centre northward. Islamic civilisation preserved Greek learning that later revived European thought. The Early Middle Ages thus saw the creation of three civilisations - Latin Christian, Byzantine and Islamic - from the Roman world.

Early medieval society was shaped by warlords, landlords, peasants and networks of trade and gift exchange. The Carolingian realm became a major political centre, and Charlemagne's legacy influenced later European kingship.

Between 1000 and 1300 kingdoms and principalities became more institutionalised. England developed stronger political organisation, while local lordship remained important.

Population and agricultural production increased, creating conditions for wider economic and social growth.

Early medieval society: warrior aristocrats controlled land and dependent peasants; kings rewarded followers with land and gifts; Charles Martel used land grants to build cavalry. Exchange included local markets, emporia trading towns, Viking networks and gift-giving that created loyalty and obligations. Carolingian empire: Charlemagne's conquests, coronation (800), administration through counts and missi dominici, and the Carolingian Renaissance (Alcuin, minuscule script). The Treaty of Verdun (843) divided the empire, and Viking, Magyar and Saracen invasions encouraged local lordship.

Kingdoms and principalities 1000-1300: the Capetian kings of France (from 987) gradually extended royal power (Philip II Augustus); the Holy Roman Empire (from 962) struggled with the papacy and local princes; England developed a strong monarchy after 1066 (Domesday Book, common law under Henry II, Magna Carta 1215, Parliament); the Christian kingdoms of Spain advanced in the Reconquista. Feudal relations (lords, vassals, fiefs) and manorialism (lords and serfs) organised society, though historians debate how systematic feudalism was.

Economic growth: agricultural innovations (heavy plough, horse collar, three-field rotation, mills), forest clearance and colonisation, a warmer climate and peace led to population growth, which in turn stimulated the commercial revolution, urban growth and cultural flowering of the High Middle Ages.

The Central Middle Ages saw religious reform, stronger papal claims and renewal in monastic life. Western Europe also became more expansionist.

The Crusades created Christian states and colonies in parts of the eastern Mediterranean. At the same time, commercial expansion, better transport and the commercialisation of the countryside changed the economy.

Universities, towns and urban society grew, while late medieval humanism contributed to new intellectual developments.

Religious reform: the Cluniac reform (from 910) and Gregorian reform (eleventh century) fought simony, lay investiture and clerical marriage; the Investiture Controversy (Gregory VII vs Henry IV, Canossa 1077, Concordat of Worms 1122); papal monarchy under Innocent III (Fourth Lateran Council, 1215); new orders - Cistercians, and the mendicant Franciscans and Dominicans who preached in towns; and campaigns against heresy (the Cathars, the Inquisition).

Expansion: the Crusades (1095-1291) established Crusader states in the Levant and colonies of Italian merchants; the Reconquista in Spain (Toledo 1085, Las Navas de Tolosa 1212); German eastward settlement; and the Normans in Sicily and southern Italy. Commercial revolution: Italian trade with the East, Flemish cloth industry, the Champagne fairs, the Hanseatic League, banking, bills of exchange and gold coins, and the commercialisation of the countryside.

Universities and towns: Bologna, Paris and Oxford became centres of learning; scholasticism (Abelard, Aquinas) combined Christian theology with Aristotle; Gothic cathedrals (Chartres, Notre-Dame) expressed religious and urban pride. Towns obtained charters, guilds organised economic life, and a bourgeoisie emerged. Late medieval humanism (Petrarch, Boccaccio, Bruni) began to revive classical learning. The Central Middle Ages were therefore a period of growth, confidence and creativity.

From about 1300 to 1500 Europe experienced major crises. War, famine and pestilence caused severe demographic and social disruption. Economic contraction affected many areas, although change varied by region.

Social contrasts and conflicts became sharper in some places. States continued to consolidate, while the Church faced serious institutional crisis.

The Great Schism and conciliar movement challenged papal authority. These developments formed part of the transition from medieval Europe toward the early modern age.

Crisis: the Great Famine (1315-1317), the Black Death (1347-1351, killing a third or more of the population) and recurring plagues, and the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) devastated Europe. Economic contraction, abandonment of villages, labour shortages and higher wages followed; lords tried to keep wages low (the Statute of Labourers, 1351, in England), leading to revolts such as the Jacquerie (1358), the English Peasants' Revolt (1381) and the Ciompi revolt (1378). Serfdom declined in western Europe but strengthened in eastern Europe.

State consolidation: the monarchies of France (after the Hundred Years' War), England (after the Wars of the Roses, 1455-1485, under the Tudors), and Spain (union of Castile and Aragon through Ferdinand and Isabella, 1469; conquest of Granada, 1492) became stronger, with standing armies, taxation and bureaucracies. The Ottomans captured Constantinople (1453).

Church crisis: the Avignon papacy (1309-1377), the Great Schism (1378-1417) and the conciliar movement (Councils of Constance and Basel) weakened papal authority. Critics such as John Wycliffe (Lollards) and Jan Hus (Hussites) attacked church corruption. At the same time, humanism, printing (Gutenberg, c. 1450) and the voyages of discovery (Columbus, 1492; Vasco da Gama, 1498) marked the transition to the early modern age.
Environmental history studies changing relationships between human societies and the natural world over time.

Environmental history emerged as a field in the 1970s, especially in the USA, influenced by the environmental movement (Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring', 1962, about pesticides). Pioneers include Donald Worster ('Dust Bowl', 1979), William Cronon ('Changes in the Land', 1983), Alfred Crosby ('The Columbian Exchange', 1972, 'Ecological Imperialism', 1986) and, in France, the Annales school (Fernand Braudel, Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie on climate history).

Worster described three levels: (1) the study of nature itself in the past (ecosystems, climate); (2) the socio-economic realm, how people used and changed the environment through technology and production; and (3) the realm of ideas, perceptions, ethics and laws about nature. In India, Madhav Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha ('This Fissured Land', 1992), Ramachandra Guha ('The Unquiet Woods', 1989) and Mahesh Rangarajan are key environmental historians.
Environmental history draws from history as well as ecology, geography, anthropology and other fields to understand human-environment relations.

Environmental history uses evidence and methods from many disciplines: ecology (ecosystems, food chains, biodiversity), geography (landscapes, climate, soils), geology, botany and zoology (pollen analysis, tree rings - dendrochronology - and ice cores to reconstruct past climates), anthropology (how communities use resources and their beliefs about nature), economics, sociology, archaeology and political science.

This approach helps explain, for example, how deforestation affected rainfall and soil erosion, how diseases spread with colonial conquest (the Columbian Exchange), and how famine was linked to both climate (El Niño droughts) and colonial policy (Mike Davis, 'Late Victorian Holocausts', 2001). It also uses traditional historical sources - government records, travellers' accounts, forest department reports, folk songs and oral histories.
Ecology studies relationships among organisms and their surroundings. Environmental history uses ecological knowledge to interpret historical change.

The term 'ecology' was coined by the German biologist Ernst Haeckel in 1866 (from Greek oikos, household). An ecosystem consists of living organisms (biotic components - producers, consumers, decomposers) and their physical environment (abiotic - air, water, soil, sunlight) interacting through energy flows and nutrient cycles. Key concepts include carrying capacity, biodiversity, ecological balance, succession and the food chain.

The environment includes all natural and human-made surroundings. Environmental historians use ecological concepts to understand how human actions - hunting, farming, deforestation, irrigation, industry and urbanisation - changed ecosystems, and how environmental changes in turn affected societies. Ecology also inspired philosophies such as 'deep ecology' (Arne Naess), which values nature for its own sake.
The 1972 Stockholm Conference and Declaration marked an important stage in international environmental awareness and cooperation.

The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment was held in Stockholm, Sweden, from 5 to 16 June 1972 - the first major global conference on the environment. India's Prime Minister Indira Gandhi spoke, famously linking poverty and environment ('Are not poverty and need the greatest polluters?'). 5 June is celebrated as World Environment Day.

The Stockholm Declaration contained 26 principles, including the human right to a healthy environment, the responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future generations, the conservation of natural resources and wildlife, the control of pollution, and the sovereign right of states to exploit their resources without causing damage to others. It led to the creation of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP, headquartered in Nairobi). Later milestones include the Brundtland Report (1987, 'sustainable development'), the Rio Earth Summit (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015). In India, the Department of Environment (1980), the Water Act (1974), the Air Act (1981) and the Environment (Protection) Act (1986) followed.
Hunting-gathering societies depended directly on wild plants and animals and represent an early form of human adaptation to the environment.

For most of human history (over 95 percent), people lived by hunting animals, fishing and gathering wild plants, fruits, nuts and roots. Hunter-gatherers lived in small, mobile bands, moving with the seasons and the availability of resources. They had detailed knowledge of their environment and generally had a relatively low impact on it.

However, they did change environments: they used fire to clear vegetation and drive game, and some historians argue that early humans contributed to the extinction of large animals (megafauna) in Australia and the Americas ('Pleistocene overkill' theory). Anthropologist Marshall Sahlins called hunter-gatherers 'the original affluent society' because their needs were few and easily met. In India, some communities such as the Chenchus, Birhors and the Andaman islanders continued hunting-gathering into modern times.
Pastoral societies depended heavily on domesticated animals and often moved according to seasonal needs and resources.

Pastoralism developed after the domestication of animals (sheep, goats, cattle, camels, horses, yaks, reindeer). Pastoral nomads move with their herds in search of pasture and water, often following seasonal patterns (transhumance - moving between summer pastures in the mountains and winter pastures in the plains). Examples include the Mongols and other steppe peoples, the Bedouins of Arabia, the Maasai of East Africa and, in India, the Gujjars and Bakarwals of Jammu and Kashmir, the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh, the Raikas (Rebaris) of Rajasthan and the Dhangars of Maharashtra.

Pastoralism allowed people to use dry grasslands and mountains unsuitable for farming. Overgrazing could cause land degradation, but pastoralists also had traditional systems to manage pastures. Relations with farmers included both exchange (manure for crops) and conflict. Colonial rule restricted pastoral movement through forest laws, grazing taxes and the Criminal Tribes Act (1871), which labelled some nomadic groups as criminals.
Settled agriculture transformed landscapes through cultivation, permanent settlements and increasing control over land and water.

The Neolithic Revolution, beginning around 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent of West Asia and independently in China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and parts of Africa and India, led to farming and permanent villages. Agriculture produced surplus food, supported larger populations, cities, states, social classes, writing and specialisation.

It also transformed environments: forests were cleared, land was ploughed, rivers were diverted for irrigation, and wild plants and animals were replaced by domesticated ones. Environmental problems included soil erosion, salinisation of irrigated land (contributing to the decline of Mesopotamian agriculture), deforestation and new diseases from living close to animals. Historians such as Jared Diamond ('Guns, Germs, and Steel', 1997) called agriculture 'the worst mistake in the history of the human race' in terms of health and inequality, although this view is debated.
Industrial production greatly increased resource extraction, energy use, pollution and human capacity to transform nature.

The Industrial Revolution, beginning in Britain around 1760, used fossil fuels - coal, and later oil and gas - to power machines, factories, railways and steamships. It led to rapid urbanisation, population growth, mass production and consumption. Environmental effects included air pollution (smog in London; the 1952 Great Smog killed thousands), water pollution, deforestation, mining damage, loss of biodiversity and the rise of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, causing global warming.

In the twentieth century, chemicals (DDT, as exposed in 'Silent Spring'), nuclear technology, plastics and industrial agriculture created new problems. Industrial disasters such as the Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984, the Union Carbide methyl isocyanate leak that killed thousands) and Chernobyl (1986) showed the dangers. Scientists now speak of the 'Anthropocene', a geological age in which humans are the main force changing the planet. Climate change is the most serious environmental crisis of our time.
The syllabus begins colonial environmental history with the pre-colonial scenario to provide a background for later changes in resource control.

Before colonial rule, Indian forests were used by many communities - tribal groups practising shifting cultivation, hunting and gathering, pastoralists, peasants who collected fuel, fodder and timber, and artisans who used forest products. Use was regulated by local customs and community institutions; sacred groves (devrais in Maharashtra, kavus in Kerala, the sacred forests of Mawphlang in Meghalaya) were protected, and in Mizoram village chiefs set aside protected forest land around villages.

Rulers also used forests for hunting, elephants and timber, and sometimes cleared them for agriculture and revenue. Madhav Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha argued that pre-colonial India had relatively sustainable resource use with community control; critics (for example, Sumit Guha) argue that pre-colonial states also exploited forests and that the picture should not be idealised. Nonetheless, colonial rule marked a major break by asserting state monopoly over forests.
Colonial policies treated forests and other resources as important sources of revenue and strategic material.

The British saw India's forests primarily as a commercial resource. Initially, they cleared forests for agriculture to increase land revenue and for plantations (tea in Assam and the Nilgiris, coffee, indigo). From the mid-nineteenth century, timber was in great demand, and forests were rapidly depleted. Valuable species such as teak, sal, deodar and sandalwood were exploited.

Wildlife was also exploited: colonial officials and princes hunted tigers, leopards and elephants on a massive scale, and rewards were given for killing 'vermin' (tigers, wolves); tens of thousands of tigers were killed between 1875 and 1925. Mining (coal, iron, manganese) and the extension of commercial agriculture also transformed landscapes. Colonial resource exploitation thus served imperial economic and strategic needs.
Demand for timber for shipbuilding and railways contributed to intensified pressure on forests.

In the early nineteenth century, oak forests in England were depleted, and the Royal Navy needed timber for ships. Indian teak from Malabar and Burma was strong and durable, and large quantities were cut; the British built ships in Bombay and elsewhere. The first teak plantation was established at Nilambur in Kerala (1840s) by H. V. Conolly.

From the 1850s, the railways created huge demand for wooden sleepers - each mile of track needed about 1,760-2,000 sleepers - and for fuel wood for locomotives. By the 1890s, about a million sleepers were required every year. Forests around railway lines in the Himalayas, central India and the south were cleared. Lord Dalhousie's 1855 forest charter and the concern about forest destruction led to the creation of the Forest Department.
Wartime demand increased pressure on forest resources and linked local environments to imperial military needs.

During the First World War (1914-1918) and the Second World War (1939-1945), the British needed huge amounts of timber for military purposes - for ships, railway sleepers, ammunition boxes, aircraft, buildings, fuel and paper. The Forest Department increased cutting far beyond sustainable levels, especially in the Himalayan forests, central India and Burma.

War also increased demand for bamboo, resin, tannins and other forest products, and in the Second World War, north-east India and Burma became war zones (the Imphal and Kohima battles of 1944), leading to clearance of forests for roads and camps. After the wars, forests were seriously degraded. The wars thus linked local environments to the global imperial war economy.
Colonial forest reservation and laws increased state control over forests and affected communities that depended on forest resources.

In 1864, the Imperial Forest Department was established with the German forester Dietrich Brandis as the first Inspector-General of Forests. The Indian Forest Act of 1865 was followed by the more comprehensive Indian Forest Act of 1878, which classified forests into three categories: reserved forests (the best, where villagers had almost no rights), protected forests (with some customary rights recorded and regulated) and village forests. The Indian Forest Act of 1927 consolidated these laws. The Forest Research Institute was set up at Dehradun (1906).

Effects: forest communities lost access to forests for fuel, fodder, grazing, food and timber; shifting cultivation (jhum, podu, bewar) was restricted or banned; hunting was prohibited for villagers while it remained a sport for elites; forest officials and guards harassed villagers; and many forest-dwellers became labourers for the forest department. This led to resistance, such as the Bastar rebellion (1910), the revolts in Kumaon and Garhwal (forest fires, 1916-1921), the Rampa rebellion of Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922-1924) in Andhra and forest satyagrahas during the national movement. After independence, the National Forest Policy (1952, 1988) and the Forest Rights Act (2006) tried to address these issues.
The Chipko Movement became an important environmental movement associated with local resistance to commercial forest exploitation.

The Chipko ('to hug' or 'to stick') movement began in 1973 at Mandal village in Chamoli district, Garhwal (now Uttarakhand), when villagers led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt of the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh prevented a sports goods company from cutting ash trees by threatening to hug them. In 1974, at Reni village, women led by Gaura Devi hugged trees to stop loggers while the men were away. The movement was inspired by Gandhian non-violence and the earlier sacrifice of the Bishnoi community at Khejarli (Rajasthan, 1730), when Amrita Devi and 363 people died protecting trees.

Sunderlal Bahuguna spread the movement through padyatras and the slogan 'Ecology is permanent economy'. In 1980, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a fifteen-year ban on commercial felling in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh. Chipko is significant as a peasant and women's movement for the right to use local resources, and it inspired the Appiko movement in Karnataka (1983). Ramachandra Guha's 'The Unquiet Woods' studied it.
The movement raised questions about large dams, displacement, development and environmental justice.

The Sardar Sarovar Project on the Narmada river in Gujarat, part of a plan for about 30 large dams on the Narmada (in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat), was intended to provide irrigation, drinking water (to Kutch and Saurashtra) and electricity. Critics pointed out that it would displace hundreds of thousands of people, mostly tribals and peasants, submerge forests and fertile land, and that resettlement was inadequate.

The Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA, 'Save the Narmada Movement') was formed in 1989, led by Medha Patkar and supported by Baba Amte, Arundhati Roy and others. It used rallies, hunger strikes, jal samadhi (threatening to drown in rising waters) and court cases. The World Bank withdrew funding in 1993 after the Morse Committee's independent review. The Supreme Court allowed construction to continue in 2000 with conditions for rehabilitation; the dam was completed and inaugurated in 2017. The NBA raised fundamental questions about development, displacement and environmental justice.
Campaigns in Kerala opposed a major project that threatened the Silent Valley ecosystem and became important in Indian environmental activism.

Silent Valley in Palakkad district, Kerala, is one of the last undisturbed tropical evergreen rainforests in the Western Ghats, home to rare species such as the lion-tailed macaque. In the 1970s, the Kerala State Electricity Board proposed a hydroelectric dam on the Kunthipuzha river, which would submerge part of the forest.

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP, a people's science movement), scientists (Salim Ali), poets (Sugathakumari, whose poem 'Marathinu Stuthi' - Ode to a Tree - became the movement's anthem), and international conservationists campaigned against it from 1973. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi intervened, and the project was dropped in 1983. Silent Valley was declared a National Park in 1984 (inaugurated 1985). It was one of India's first successful environmental campaigns and showed the role of scientists and citizens in conservation.
The Plachimada struggle in Kerala raised concerns over groundwater, corporate activity and local community rights.

In 2000, Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages set up a bottling plant at Plachimada in Palakkad district, Kerala. Local residents, mostly Dalit and Adivasi farmers and labourers, complained that the plant's extraction of groundwater dried up wells and that the remaining water became polluted; the company also distributed sludge as fertiliser, which was found to contain toxic heavy metals (cadmium and lead), according to a BBC report (2003).

Protests began in April 2002, led by Mylamma, an Adivasi woman, and others, with sit-ins outside the factory. The Perumatty gram panchayat cancelled the plant's licence (2003), leading to court cases on whether a local body can control groundwater use (the Kerala High Court initially supported the panchayat). The plant stopped production in 2004. In 2011 the Kerala Assembly passed a bill to set up a tribunal for compensation. The issue raised questions about corporate use of natural resources, groundwater as a common resource, and the rights of local communities.
Environmental history examines how marginalised communities experience resource control, displacement and ecological change.

Environmental historians and activists emphasise that environmental problems affect the poor and marginalised most severely - tribal communities displaced by dams, mines and wildlife sanctuaries, fishing communities affected by industrial pollution, pastoralists losing grazing land and poor urban residents living near polluted sites. Ramachandra Guha and Joan Martinez-Alier called this the 'environmentalism of the poor', which is about survival and livelihood rather than wilderness protection.

Movements such as Chipko, the NBA, the struggle of the Dongria Kondh against bauxite mining in the Niyamgiri hills (Odisha; the gram sabhas rejected Vedanta's project in 2013), and the Forest Rights Act (2006), which recognises the rights of forest-dwellers, show the voices of the margins. Environmental history aims to include these perspectives and to recognise indigenous knowledge of ecosystems.
Women often have distinct relationships with local resources through livelihood and household responsibilities, making gender important in environmental movements and history.

Women in rural India often collect fuel, fodder and water, gather forest produce and manage household food, so deforestation and water scarcity increase their workload directly. This explains women's leadership in movements like Chipko (Gaura Devi), Plachimada (Mylamma) and the NBA (Medha Patkar).

Ecofeminism links the domination of women and nature by patriarchal and capitalist systems. Vandana Shiva ('Staying Alive', 1988) argued that women are closer to nature and protect it, and that Western development models destroy both. Critics such as Bina Agarwal proposed 'feminist environmentalism', arguing that women's relationship with nature comes from their material roles and social position, not from any inherent nature. Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement in Kenya (Nobel Peace Prize, 2004) is another example of women leading environmental action.

sections.title: Meaning and Scope of Environmental History

blocks.text:
Environmental history examines the changing relationship between humans and nature. It is interdisciplinary because historical explanation may require knowledge from ecology, geography and other fields.

The course introduces ecology and environment and also includes the United Nations and the Stockholm Declaration. This shows how environmental history connects long-term human experience with modern global environmental concern.

Definition and scope: environmental history studies the interaction between human societies and the natural world over time - how nature shaped human history (climate, disease, resources, geography) and how humans changed nature (agriculture, deforestation, industry, urbanisation). It also studies how people thought about nature (religion, science, aesthetics, law). Donald Worster's three levels - nature itself, socio-economic use and ideas - define its scope.

Interdisciplinary approach: it draws on ecology, geography, biology, climatology, anthropology, economics and archaeology, using sources such as pollen records, tree rings, ice cores, forest department reports, travellers' accounts and oral traditions. Ecological concepts like ecosystems, carrying capacity and biodiversity help explain historical changes.

Global awareness: the 1972 Stockholm Conference (the UN Conference on the Human Environment), its Declaration of 26 principles and the creation of UNEP marked the beginning of international environmental cooperation. Indira Gandhi linked poverty with environmental degradation. Later developments included the Brundtland Report (1987) defining sustainable development, the Rio Earth Summit (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015). In India, environmental laws and the Ministry of Environment and Forests (1985) followed. Environmental history thus connects past and present concerns.

Human relationships with nature changed from hunting and gathering to pastoralism, settled agriculture and industrial society. Each form of subsistence created different environmental pressures.

Agriculture transformed land and settlement patterns, while industrialisation greatly increased extraction, energy consumption and pollution.

The syllabus uses this long historical sequence to explain that environmental crisis has historical roots and cannot be understood only as a recent issue.

Hunting and gathering: for most of human existence, people lived in small mobile bands with low environmental impact, though they used fire and may have contributed to megafaunal extinctions. Pastoralism: the domestication of animals allowed people to use grasslands and mountains; nomadic and transhumant pastoralists managed pastures but could cause overgrazing. Settled agriculture (from about 10,000 years ago) led to surplus, population growth, villages, cities and states, but also deforestation, soil erosion, salinisation and the spread of diseases.

Industrialisation (from the eighteenth century) used fossil fuels and machines, causing massive increases in resource extraction, energy use, pollution, urbanisation and population. In the twentieth century, chemical agriculture, plastics and nuclear technology added new dangers; disasters like Bhopal (1984) and Chernobyl (1986) showed the risks. Climate change from greenhouse gases is now the greatest environmental threat.

Analysis: each stage increased human ability to change nature and the scale of environmental impact. Colonialism spread European agriculture, plantations and resource exploitation across the world (Crosby's 'ecological imperialism'). The environmental crisis thus has deep historical roots in changing modes of production and consumption, and understanding this history helps in seeking sustainable solutions.

The course compares the pre-colonial background with colonial changes. Imperial governments increasingly sought systematic control over natural resources.

Timber demand for shipbuilding and railways increased pressure on forests. The World Wars created further demand. Forest reservation and legislation strengthened state authority over forest resources.

These policies also affected communities whose livelihoods depended on forests, making colonial environmental history a history of both resources and power.

Pre-colonial scenario: forests were used by communities for shifting cultivation, hunting, gathering, grazing and crafts under customary rules and sacred groves; rulers hunted and used timber, but there was no centralised state monopoly. Historians debate whether this was a sustainable 'golden age' (Gadgil and Guha) or included its own forms of exploitation.

Colonial exploitation: forests were cleared for agriculture and plantations to increase revenue; teak was cut for the Royal Navy (shipbuilding); railways from the 1850s demanded millions of sleepers and fuel; the World Wars required huge amounts of timber and forest products. Colonial forest policy: the Forest Department (1864, Brandis), the Indian Forest Acts of 1865, 1878 and 1927, the division into reserved, protected and village forests, and the 'scientific forestry' of commercial plantations (teak, sal, pine) replacing mixed natural forests.

Impact on communities: restrictions on access to forests, bans on shifting cultivation and hunting, forced labour, harassment by forest guards, and the classification of some communities as 'criminal tribes'. Resistance included the Bastar revolt (1910), Rampa rebellion (1922-1924), Kumaon and Garhwal forest protests, and forest satyagrahas. Colonial environmental history thus shows how control over nature was linked with state power, revenue and the marginalisation of forest-dependent people.

The syllabus includes Chipko, Narmada Bachao Andolan, Silent Valley and the Plachimada issue. These movements raised questions about forests, dams, water, development and community rights.

Environmental history also gives attention to voices from the margins and to women. This is important because the costs and benefits of environmental change are not distributed equally.

Indian environmental movements therefore connect ecology with livelihood, social justice and political participation.

Chipko (1973 onwards, Garhwal): villagers, especially women (Gaura Devi), hugged trees to stop commercial logging; leaders Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna; led to a ban on green felling in the Himalayas (1980). Silent Valley (1973-1983, Kerala): scientists, KSSP and poets successfully opposed a hydroelectric project, leading to a National Park (1984). Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985/1989 onwards): Medha Patkar and others opposed large dams that would displace people and submerge land; the World Bank withdrew (1993), but the Sardar Sarovar dam was completed (2017). Plachimada (2002 onwards, Kerala): Adivasi and Dalit residents, led by Mylamma, fought against Coca-Cola's groundwater extraction and pollution; the plant closed in 2004.

Voices from the margins: these movements highlight the 'environmentalism of the poor' - struggles for livelihood, land and water by tribal people, peasants, fishers and the urban poor, who bear the costs of development while the benefits go elsewhere. The Forest Rights Act (2006) and the Niyamgiri case (2013) recognised the rights of forest communities. Women and environment: women's daily dependence on fuel, fodder and water explains their leadership; ecofeminism (Vandana Shiva) and feminist environmentalism (Bina Agarwal) offer different explanations.

Significance: Indian environmental movements linked ecology with social justice, democracy and development. They used Gandhian non-violent methods, legal action and public campaigns, and influenced laws and policies (environmental impact assessments, the National Green Tribunal, 2010). They show that environmental issues are also questions of who controls resources.
